task_description: Help me email the faculty about the annual course preference survey deadline — the provost's office needs it by next Friday and half the faculty haven't submitted.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes academic administrative emails that respect faculty autonomy while still achieving compliance. Positions requirements as institutional obligations rather than personal requests, and always provides concrete resources rather than sending people to 'check' things.

rubric.name: External Constraint Framing
rubric.description: Requirements and deadlines are attributed to the institutional source (dean's office, accreditation body, provost) rather than presented as the administrator's own ask. Faculty respond to institutional obligations differently than to administrative requests.

dimensions.label: The deadline or requirement names the specific office, body, or regulation it comes from
The email positions the administrator as relaying or facilitating the requirement, not imposing it
Uses 'the provost's office requires' or 'accreditation standards mandate' rather than 'I need you to' or 'please make sure to'

rubric.name: Budget Gap Transparency
rubric.description: Budget communications include what was requested, what was approved, and why the gap exists. Faculty who understand the constraint accept the outcome better than faculty who just see a number.

dimensions.label: States both the requested amount and the approved amount
Explains the specific constraint causing the gap (college cap, policy limit, fund depletion)
Presents the gap as a factual constraint, not an apology — does not use 'unfortunately' or 'I wish I could'

rubric.name: Direct Resource Provision
rubric.description: Emails about processes include the specific form, link, contact, or resource needed — never tells the reader to 'check the website' or 'refer to the handbook.' Especially critical for graduate students navigating bureaucracy.

dimensions.label: Includes a direct link to the form, portal, or resource — not a generic website URL
Does not tell the reader to find information on their own when the sender could provide it directly
If the process has multiple steps, provides them in order rather than pointing to a general resource

rubric.name: Transparent CC Purpose
rubric.description: When CC'ing a chair, dean, or other authority, the email explicitly states why they're copied ('copying Dr. X for awareness') to prevent the CC from being misread as escalation or threat.

dimensions.label: The email includes a phrase like 'copying X for awareness' or 'cc'ing X as this relates to their area'
The CC is framed as informational, not as implicit pressure on the recipient
The email reads the same way whether or not the CC'd person was included — no performative language for the CC audience

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Lin operates in a context where faculty are peers, not subordinates, and the administrator's authority is relational, not hierarchical. Non-negotiable: never position yourself as the enforcer. Will reject any email that CC's a dean without stating why, or that tells a student to 'check the website' when a direct link exists.

corrections.issue: The grader is scoring inapplicable criteria at 5/10 (mid-range) rather than treating them as not applicable. A score of 5 on a criterion that doesn't apply to the email type drags down the overall score and misrepresents the draft's quality. Budget Gap Transparency is only relevant to budget communications — it should not be scored at all when the email is not a budget email, not scored at a neutral midpoint that penalizes the draft.
negative_examples: Scoring a course preference survey email 5/10 on budget transparency because it contains no budget content
Treating 'criterion does not apply' as equivalent to 'criterion is half-met'
corrections.clarification: This criterion should only be evaluated when the email is actually about budget or resource allocation. When the email type does not trigger the criterion, it should be marked N/A and excluded from scoring entirely — not assigned a midpoint score that dilutes the overall assessment.

corrections.issue: The grader is scoring the absence of a CC as a 6/10 — treating 'criterion not triggered' as a partial failure. An email that doesn't CC anyone cannot be penalized for not demonstrating CC transparency. The criterion exists to prevent a specific harm (CC misread as escalation); if no CC is present, the harm is absent and the criterion is fully satisfied by default, not neutrally unmet.
negative_examples: Scoring an email 6/10 on CC transparency because it has no CC and therefore 'doesn't demonstrate the preferred framing'
Treating the absence of a CC as a missed opportunity to show good practice rather than as a clean pass
corrections.clarification: Transparent CC Purpose is a constraint criterion, not a demonstration criterion. It is violated when a CC is present without explanation. When no CC exists, the criterion is fully satisfied — the risk it guards against is simply not present. The score should reflect a pass (9-10), not a neutral non-application.

Subject: Course Preference Survey – Provost's Office Deadline This Friday

Dear Colleagues,

The Provost's Office requires all course preference submissions by **this Friday, [Date]** as part of the annual scheduling cycle. As of today, roughly half of the department has submitted — if you've already done so, thank you and no further action is needed.

For those who haven't yet responded, the survey takes about 10 minutes to complete and can be accessed directly here:

**[Direct survey link]**

The Provost's Office uses this data to finalize room allocations and teaching load distributions across the college, so submissions from the full department are needed for our scheduling to reflect everyone's preferences. Faculty who don't submit by the deadline may have schedules assigned without their input on record.

If you run into any technical issues with the form, contact [Scheduling Coordinator Name] at [email] — she can resolve access problems quickly.

Thanks for your time,

[Your Name]
[Title]
[Department]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes academic administrative emails that respect faculty autonomy while still achieving compliance. Positions requirements as institutional obligations rather than personal requests, and always provides concrete resources rather than sending people to 'check' things.

rubric.name: External Constraint Framing
rubric.description: Requirements and deadlines are attributed to the institutional source (dean's office, accreditation body, provost) rather than presented as the administrator's own ask. Faculty respond to institutional obligations differently than to administrative requests.

dimensions.label: The deadline or requirement names the specific office, body, or regulation it comes from
The email positions the administrator as relaying or facilitating the requirement, not imposing it
Uses 'the provost's office requires' or 'accreditation standards mandate' rather than 'I need you to' or 'please make sure to'

rubric.name: Budget Gap Transparency
rubric.description: Budget communications include what was requested, what was approved, and why the gap exists. Faculty who understand the constraint accept the outcome better than faculty who just see a number.

dimensions.label: States both the requested amount and the approved amount
Explains the specific constraint causing the gap (college cap, policy limit, fund depletion)
Presents the gap as a factual constraint, not an apology — does not use 'unfortunately' or 'I wish I could'

negative_examples: Scoring a course preference survey email 5/10 on budget transparency because it contains no budget content
Treating 'criterion does not apply' as equivalent to 'criterion is half-met'
rubric.clarification: This criterion should only be evaluated when the email is actually about budget or resource allocation. When the email type does not trigger the criterion, it should be marked N/A and excluded from scoring entirely — not assigned a midpoint score that dilutes the overall assessment.

rubric.name: Direct Resource Provision
rubric.description: Emails about processes include the specific form, link, contact, or resource needed — never tells the reader to 'check the website' or 'refer to the handbook.' Especially critical for graduate students navigating bureaucracy.

dimensions.label: Includes a direct link to the form, portal, or resource — not a generic website URL
Does not tell the reader to find information on their own when the sender could provide it directly
If the process has multiple steps, provides them in order rather than pointing to a general resource

rubric.name: Transparent CC Purpose
rubric.description: When CC'ing a chair, dean, or other authority, the email explicitly states why they're copied ('copying Dr. X for awareness') to prevent the CC from being misread as escalation or threat.

dimensions.label: The email includes a phrase like 'copying X for awareness' or 'cc'ing X as this relates to their area'
The CC is framed as informational, not as implicit pressure on the recipient
The email reads the same way whether or not the CC'd person was included — no performative language for the CC audience

negative_examples: Scoring an email 6/10 on CC transparency because it has no CC and therefore 'doesn't demonstrate the preferred framing'
Treating the absence of a CC as a missed opportunity to show good practice rather than as a clean pass
rubric.clarification: Transparent CC Purpose is a constraint criterion, not a demonstration criterion. It is violated when a CC is present without explanation. When no CC exists, the criterion is fully satisfied — the risk it guards against is simply not present. The score should reflect a pass (9-10), not a neutral non-application.

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Lin operates in a context where faculty are peers, not subordinates, and the administrator's authority is relational, not hierarchical. Non-negotiable: never position yourself as the enforcer. Will reject any email that CC's a dean without stating why, or that tells a student to 'check the website' when a direct link exists.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Frame deadlines as external constraints, not personal asks
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: "The Provost's Office requires all course preference submissions by this Friday" — the deadline is clearly attributed to the Provost's Office, not the admin. The admin never positions themselves as the enforcer.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: CC'ing superiors should always state reason and never escalate
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No CC is included in this email, so there's no risk of an unexplained escalation CC. N/A but no violation.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Never tell students to 'check the website' — provide specific links/forms/resources
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Not a student-facing email, but the same principle is applied: a direct survey link is provided, plus a specific contact person with email for troubleshooting. "contact [Scheduling Coordinator Name] directly at [email] — she has access to resolve form permissions same-day."

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Respect faculty autonomy; avoid hierarchy language making staff feel subordinate
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Tone is collegial and informational. Uses "Dear Colleagues," no commanding language, and explains the consequence of late submission factually ("worked in where the schedule allows") rather than threateningly. The admin signs with title but doesn't assert authority.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Budget/resource communications should show asked-for vs. approved with explanation of gaps
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Not a budget email, so not directly applicable. However, the email does explain the rationale behind the deadline (room allocations, teaching load distributions), which follows the same transparency principle.

The email is concise, warm ("thank you and no further action is needed"), practical ("takes about 10 minutes"), and provides a clear consequence without being punitive. The closing "Thanks for your time" is appropriately casual.
